methods.label: Compare distance divided by time
methods.explanation:
Average speed is total distance divided by total time. Evelyn's point is higher and farther left than the points for Angela, Briana, and Debra. Thus she covers more distance in less time than each of those three students, so she is faster than all three.

Carla covers more distance than Evelyn, so we must also compare their times. Let \(D>0\) be the distance represented by one vertical grid interval and \(T>0\) the time represented by one horizontal grid interval. These are convenient units; no numerical axis labels are needed.

Evelyn covers more than \(4D\) in less than \(2T\). Since her time is positive, her average speed satisfies
\[
v_E>\frac{4D}{2T}=\frac{2D}{T}.
\]
Carla covers less than \(6D\) in more than \(4T\), so
\[
v_C<\frac{6D}{4T}=\frac{3D}{2T}<\frac{2D}{T}.
\]
Therefore Evelyn is faster than Carla as well. Evelyn has the greatest average speed, choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).
methods.levelReason: The method uses elementary distance-time relationships, positive-ratio comparisons, and broad bounds read from the grid. It requires no formal slope formula.

candidate.annotationRationale: The task assesses using the distance-speed-time relationship to compare average speeds. The method interprets speed as a ratio, reads distance and time from the coordinate graph, and compares positive fractions using bounds. These supporting skills do not require assigning formal linear-function or trigonometric slope nodes. The annotations describe the mathematics used, not demonstrated student mastery.
limitations: The axes have no numerical scale labels, so exact physical speeds cannot be calculated. The plotted ratios still determine their ordering.

review.mathematicalCheck: The visible grid gives Evelyn distance >4D and time <2T, so her speed exceeds 2D/T. Carla's distance <6D and time >4T give speed <3D/(2T). Evelyn also travels farther in less time than each remaining student, establishing a unique maximum.
